doc.title: David Torkanowsky interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019

title: Studio philosophy: real over perfect, and 'Green Onions'
summary: He hires players who already sound right, prefers imperfect live takes, and discusses Booker T's record and tape versus ProTools.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Yeah. I mean I’ve fired people from studio recording sessions but never fired them and not paid them. It’s just like in the studio, and I learned this from George Duke, you don’t hire a musician and then try to get them to play how you want in the studio, you get musicians that already play how you want. Because otherwise you’re not going to get — I mean my mantra in the studio is it doesn’t have to sound good. It just has to sound real. You know some of the best — what are the best music recordings live? Because it’s real. It’s not like, “Take seven.” Or let’s comp this solo together. It’s human and it’s real. So I’ve only replaced people on recordings. I’ve never really replaced people on the gig unless they’re unreliable or show up late or show up fucked up, or I should say too fucked up. So yeah, I haven’t done it. I always —like Walter Lastie told me a long time ago, if you keep fast company you get fast. So I always try to hire the best musicians possible.
Okay here’s a really personal question. What do you think of the record “Green Onions?”
I mean it’s classic. I fucking love that record. I love it.

The reason I thought of it is because you said it just has to sound real. And I’m so fascinated by that record because like first of all it’s just got that sound, but when Steve Cropper comes in on his solo it’s like really too loud and then it gets too soft, and then it gets just right. And I was thinking man, if they had said, “Look the balance is off, do it again, do it five more times.”

I love people that make records and leave mistakes on their records. I love that. It’s just like come on — it’s a snapshot in time, and it’s again, where intent trumps execution. I try not to work in the studio with any engineer that doesn’t know what this is [gestures]. “Where’s the guitar solo, where’s the guitar solo, oh it’s around my neck.” You know? I mean we can all perform meticulously perfect sonic surgery with ProTools and I’ve used ProTools as well. But, ‘cause it’s a studio standard and it’s great, it’s multi-tracks © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

everybody can afford. But the process is nothing that sounds like tape. There’s nothing that sounds like vinyl. It’s just, come on. I don’t want to hear decoded zeroes and ones, when I can hear etched lacquer.
I remember the first time I saw that in the studio though I go what are you doing? You’re cutting the tape.
Right. Right. Based on where that kick drum is, oh there it is, mark it.
